solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: St Petersburg museum wasted millions in legacy

indicators.note: what is wasted is thrown away and lost, so those letters disappear from the word

blocks.note: the Hermitage is the great art museum in St Petersburg
M is the standard abbreviation for million(s)

explanation.surface: A Russian museum has squandered a fortune that was left to it in a bequest.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the M out of HERMITAGE and HERITAGE is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A heritage is what is handed down from earlier generations, which is exactly what a legacy is.

clue.text: Curry ingredient, a fine old eastern note carried by supermarket

indicators.note: what is carried is held inside its carrier, so one set of letters sits within another

blocks.note: taken as written
F is the pencil-grade and crossword abbreviation for fine
O is a standard abbreviation for old
E for eastern, as on a compass
ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
Asda is a large British supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A shopper picks up an exotic spice for a curry from the supermarket shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: Asda is a British supermarket chain; the five small pieces string together and sit inside its name. Ti is the sol-fa note also spelt te.
explanation.definitionFit: Asafoetida is a pungent resin powder used as a flavouring in Indian cooking, especially curries and dals.

clue.text: Revolutionary Labour on the rise? — cobblers

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom up, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a red is a revolutionary leftist
Lab is the standard abbreviation for the Labour Party
the punctuation mark printed in the clue is itself a dash

explanation.surface: A sceptic dismisses talk of a resurgent hard-left Labour Party as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the clue looks like mere punctuation but is part of the wordplay, read literally as DASH. 'Cobblers' is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British words for nonsense or rubbish talk, so they are straightforward slang synonyms.

clue.text: Sticks up, wearing self- satisfied expression

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the word is written backwards

blocks.note: to gum something is to stick it

explanation.surface: Someone sticks their nose up, wearing a self-satisfied look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticks up' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'up' alone is the reversal signal and 'Sticks' is the verb GUMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Smug describes a person visibly pleased with themselves, so a smug person is wearing a complacent, pleased look.

clue.text: Head for the runway? I’m obliged, Mr President

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thank you
Xi Jinping is President of China

explanation.surface: A pilot thanks the President on board before moving the plane out for take-off.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British slang for thanks; the President is Xi of China.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft taxis when it moves slowly along the ground towards the runway before taking off.

clue.text: British colonel upset the EU, for one

indicators.note: to upset something is to tip it over, so in a down clue the letters are turned upside down

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
Col is the abbreviation for colonel

explanation.surface: A British army colonel is angry about the European Union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the colonel's mood; it turns COL over to LOC.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of countries allied for common purposes, and the European Union is one such grouping.

clue.text: Expel Nazi extremists in party

indicators.note: extremes are the ends, so only the outside letters of the word are used
one thing being in another means it is placed inside

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
a bash is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A political party throws out its far-right extremists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' sounds like a description of Nazis, but it just takes the ends of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To banish someone is to send them away or drive them out, a close synonym of expelling.

clue.text: Entertaining woman featured in Messiah/Siegfried retrospective

indicators.note: something featured in a work appears within it, so the letters are found inside the text
a retrospective looks back, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the end of the first name and the start of the second run together

explanation.surface: A female performer appears in a retrospective season of Handel and Wagner productions.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'MessiAH SIEGfried' backwards to find the answer; the slash just joins the two works.
explanation.definitionFit: A geisha is a Japanese hostess trained to entertain guests with conversation, music and dance.

clue.text: Julius — ace tenor, idle singer…

blocks.note: Julius is the setter of this puzzle, so the setter's name stands for ME
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
T is the abbreviation for tenor
to loaf is to idle about

explanation.surface: The setter introduces himself as a top tenor and a lazy singer.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter naming himself means ME. The ellipsis carries on into the next clue, whose answer is another singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat Loaf was the American rock vocalist famous for the album Bat Out of Hell.

clue.text: …one who didn’t regret nicking large part of rice dish

indicators.note: to nick is to steal, and what is stolen is taken away from the rest

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large
pilaf is a spiced rice dish

explanation.surface: Someone helps themselves to most of a plate of rice without remorse.
explanation.walkthrough: Steal the L from PILAF. Edith Piaf's signature song is 'Non, je ne regrette rien' ('No, I regret nothing'), and the ellipsis links her to the singer in the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The French chanteuse famously sang that she regretted nothing, so she is the person who had no regrets.

clue.text: Big studio ordered to bring in cold snack for Lassie

indicators.note: putting things in order means arranging them afresh, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A film studio orders in a treat for its canine star Lassie.
explanation.walkthrough: C joins the letters of BIG STUDIO and all ten are shuffled together.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassie is the famous collie of film and television, and a dog biscuit is a treat given to dogs.

clue.text: Rich European lot

blocks.note: fat means rich, as in a fat salary or rich food
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A group of wealthy Europeans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lot' looks like a noun for a group of people, but it means one's destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: One's lot in life is the fortune destiny allots, which is what fate means.

clue.text: Wary going out with hot rod? At least it’s driveable

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase; the adjective is what the clause asserts of a vehicle

indicators.note: going out suggests leaving its proper place or shape, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cautious person goes out in a souped-up car, consoling themselves that at least it runs.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of WARY and HOT ROD are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadworthy vehicle is fit and safe to be driven on public roads, the minimum one could say of it.

clue.text: Goodbye card finally that is sealed in gold envelope

indicators.note: finally points at the last letter of the word just before it
something sealed in is shut up inside a wrapper, so those letters are enclosed by others

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is
Au is the chemical symbol for gold, which here forms the outer wrapping

explanation.surface: A farewell card is posted in a golden envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: D and IE together go inside AU, the chemical symbol for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is the French farewell, borrowed into English as a formal way to bid someone farewell.

clue.text: Flinch, however put on skirts of terylene material

indicators.note: the skirts of something are its edges, so only its outer letters are taken

blocks.note: to wince is to flinch
yet can mean however or nevertheless
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone shrinks from wearing skirts made of a synthetic fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Terylene is a British brand of polyester, and 'skirts' looks like clothing but means the edges of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Winceyette is a soft brushed cotton cloth, traditionally used for nightwear and sheets, so it is a fabric.

clue.text: Bugs seen here when formatting Bible & Torah

indicators.note: formatting text lays it out anew, so the letters are put into a different arrangement

blocks.note: the two scriptures taken as written, the ampersand only joining them

explanation.surface: Software glitches turn up when typesetting scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' looks like computer errors in a formatting job, but it is Bugs Bunny, the cartoon rabbit.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugs Bunny is a cartoon rabbit, and a rabbit lives in a burrow, so that is where he would be found.

clue.text: Stupid boy’s cycling headgear

indicators.note: cycling goes round and round, so letters move from one end of the word to the other

blocks.note: in the British TV sitcom Dad's Army, Captain Mainwaring constantly calls young Private Pike 'stupid boy'

explanation.surface: A foolish lad is riding his bike in a silly hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a classic British sitcom about the wartime Home Guard. Move PI from the front of PIKE to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A kepi is a French military cap with a flat circular top and a peak, so it is a kind of hat.

clue.text: Buzz A’s commander rejected extraterrestrial life

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters are turned back to front

blocks.note: Buzz Aldrin's commander on Apollo 11 was Neil A(rmstrong)

explanation.surface: An astronaut's commanding officer dismisses the idea of life beyond Earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz A' is Buzz Aldrin, so his commander is Neil A, Neil Armstrong with the surname shortened the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: An alien is a being from another planet, the stock word for a creature from beyond Earth.

clue.text: Cry loudly, run away from fight

indicators.note: going away from something means leaving it, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
a brawl is a rough fight

explanation.surface: Someone sobs noisily and flees a scuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run away' reads as fleeing, but 'run' is R and 'away from' takes it out of BRAWL.
explanation.definitionFit: To bawl is to weep or shout noisily, as a howling child does.

clue.text: Product used for skirting wagon tax

blocks.note: a wain is an old word for a farm wagon
scot is an old word for a tax, surviving in scot-free

explanation.surface: Some product is used to dodge a tax on wagons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirting' looks like evading the tax, but it is skirting board along the bottom of a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Wainscot is wooden panelling lining the lower part of a room's walls, the material of a skirting.

clue.text: Book dull, cheerless hotel by river in York

blocks.note: bleak means dreary and cheerless
H is the NATO alphabet letter for hotel
the Ouse is the river flowing through York

explanation.surface: Someone reserves a gloomy hotel on the river in York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb for reserving the hotel; it is the definition, Dickens's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleak House is one of the major novels by Charles Dickens, about the Jarndyce lawsuit.

clue.text: German numbers Merz announced?

indicators.note: what is announced is spoken out, so the word is taken for its sound

blocks.note: Friedrich Merz is Germany's chancellor, its leader

explanation.surface: The German chancellor reads out a set of national statistics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' looks like figures but means songs; the German word for the art songs sounds like the English title for Merz.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs, such as those of Schubert, and songs are often called numbers.

clue.text: Current PM once denied greeting one of the Murdochs

indicators.note: to be denied something is to go without it, so those letters are withheld

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
Rishi Sunak was a UK prime minister
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: The current prime minister snubs a member of the Murdoch media family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current PM' reads as one phrase, but 'Current' is I and 'PM once' is the former prime minister RISHI, who loses HI.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch was the Anglo-Irish novelist and philosopher, not part of Rupert's newspaper family.

clue.text: Brought back titles penned by German writer leaving old part of Jerusalem

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run backwards
something penned is shut inside an enclosure, so it sits inside the other word
what leaves departs, so that letter drops out of the word

blocks.note: Goethe was the great German poet and dramatist
O is a standard abbreviation for old
titles are names

explanation.surface: Titles are reclaimed from a German author who has left Jerusalem's old quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old part of Jerusalem' looks like the definition, but 'old' belongs to the wordplay: it is the letter the writer loses.
explanation.definitionFit: Gethsemane is the garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem, where Jesus prayed before his arrest.

clue.text: Catch headless chicken from Australia

indicators.note: without a head means the first letter is cut off

blocks.note: chook is Australian slang for a chicken

explanation.surface: Someone catches a decapitated Australian chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the first letter of the Australian word CHOOK.
explanation.definitionFit: To hook a fish or a person is to snare them, so hook is a synonym for catch as a verb.

clue.text: Curse editor burying good article

indicators.note: to bury something is to put it inside, so letters are enclosed by others

blocks.note: ed is the abbreviation for editor
G is the abbreviation for good
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An editor swears while spiking a decent story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article A.
explanation.definitionFit: Egad is an old-fashioned mild oath, a minced form of 'by God', used as an exclamation.

clue.text: Long hour sat in American church

indicators.note: something sat in a place is inside it, so one letter goes within the others

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for American
H is the abbreviation for hour
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A long hour spent sitting in an American church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' reads as an adjective for the hour, but it is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to yearn for it, which is the verb sense of to long for something.

clue.text: Socks husband, tip of nose splits

indicators.note: to split is slang for to leave, so the named letter departs

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
taken as written
the tip is the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A husband lands a punch that splits the end of someone's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Socks' looks like a verb for punching, and 'splits' like a wound; really the first letter of NOSE leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose is an old collective word for stockings and socks, as in hosiery.

clue.text: Place for quiet contemplation; silence — not a phone is ringing

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the outer words surround the letters wanted

blocks.note: the last letters of the first word, the middle words and the start of the last run on

explanation.surface: A notice at a memorial asks for silence, as a mobile phone goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' suggests the phone, but it means surrounding: the answer sits inside 'silenCE NOT A PHone'. Britain's national war memorial on Whitehall is the Cenotaph.
explanation.definitionFit: A cenotaph is a war memorial where people gather for remembrance, notably the two minutes' silence each November.

clue.text: Grease — Travolta gutted, left depressed

indicators.note: a gutted thing has its insides removed, so only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the name
L is the abbreviation for left
low means depressed or down

explanation.surface: John Travolta, star of the film Grease, was devastated and left feeling down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grease' looks like the musical Travolta starred in, but it is the definition: a fatty substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Tallow is rendered animal fat used for candles and soap, so it is a hard grease.
